item.title: Real estate agents to face mandatory register as self-regulation
item.description:
Real estate agents to face mandatory register as self-regulation

October 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The government plans to introduce a register of real estate agents as well as a complaints desk for buyers and sellers after an investigation revealed widespread dissatisfaction with the industry.

In a letter to parliament on Thursday, housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan said the moves come after attempts to get the sector to regulate itself had failed.

“Unfortunately, I must conclude that the professional associations are unable to take the necessary further steps,” the D66 minister wrote.

Until 2001, real estate agents had to be licensed, like lawyers and architects. Currently, anyone can call themselves a real estate agent and while there are two trade organisations in the Netherlands, both say they don’t have the ability to stand up to unscrupulous agents.

“We have consistently said over the past few years that a voluntary approach does not work here. The minister is now drawing the same conclusion,” Tristan Bons, deputy director of real estate association Vastgoed Nederland said in a statement.

According to Bons, the association doesn’t have the power to punish anyone as membership is voluntary and problem agents can simply leave the group.

Nearly a third of the respondents to the government-commissioned survey had at least one negative experience with a real estate agent. Almost 90% of those complaints involved an agent affiliated with a trade association.

Just 2% of people made an official complaint. Complaints vary from passing along confidential information to driving up the price of housing.

In August, homeowners association Vereniging Eigen Huis said it had received 900 reports between February and July on a special hotline for issues with real estate agents. Issues ranged from buyers feeling pressure to bid beyond their budgets to agents favouring certain clients over others.

item.title: Dutch museum visits rose to over 30m last year
item.description:
Dutch museum visits rose to over 30m last year

October 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

More than 30 million people visited a museum in the Netherlands in 2025, a 2.5% increase over the year prior, according to trade association Museumvereniging.

Dutch museums welcomed 31.6 million visitors in 2025, almost back to pre-pandemic levels. In 2019, museums saw 32.6 million guests.

Nearly 90% of Dutch people go to a museum at least once a year, the Museumcijfers 2025 report found.

In 2025 the Netherlands had 492 registered museums. Most institutions are history museums, making up 62%, followed by art museums, which account for 24%.

The use of the yearly Museum Card hit a record high of 9.7 million visits in 2025. Visits using the subscription service is up 5% over the 2019 peak.

A recent survey by Ipsos I&O found that trust in museums is high and most adults consider them to be an important part of society.

item.title: Golf to a Japanese garden: 13 great things to do in October
item.description:
Golf to a Japanese garden: 13 great things to do in October

October 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

It’s October and the cultural season is off to a good start. There are lots of restful established names in this month’s cultural offerings, with some modern challenges mixed in.

Experience Butoh
It’s the 10th edition of the Butoh Festival at the Teatro Munganga in Amsterdam this month. Fourteen dancers from Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Italy, Mexico, Taiwan and the UK will be performing their interpretation of the avant-garde “dance of darkness”, which originated in Japan after the devastation of the atomic bombs. October 2 and 3. Website

Get your skates on for some colf
It is touted as the earliest depiction of golf: Hendrick Avercamp’s Colf Players on the Ice dating from around 1625. Then as now, the players in the foreground look like well-to-do-gentlemen while in the back two others seem to be playing a game of ice hockey.

The Rijksmuseum and the Mauritshuis have just bought the painting for an eyewatering €11.4 million from a private owner in the United States. It will go on show in Avercamp’s home town of Kampen as part of the exhibition Averkamp back in Kampen: the 17th century through the eyes of Hendrick and Barent. (Barent,  Hendrick’s nephew, also specialised in winter landscapes) From October 3. Website

Believe it (or not)
In a time when scientific fact is regarded as just another opinion, the Teylers Museum in Haarlem is mounting Zeker Weten? (Are we sure?), an exhibition around the five tenets of scientific research: prove, repeat, modify,  check and build.

That is exactly what the scientists of yore did, for instance when sightings of black swans overturned the assumption that only white ones existed, and the discovery in 1938 of a coelacanth, which proved it was not extinct. Historical books, models and instruments illustrate the search for “exact” science. From October 2. Website

Meet Matisse at the H’ART
The H’ART Museum in Amsterdam has unselfishly offered to relieve the soon-to-be refurbished Centre Pompidou of its Matisse collection, along with other paintings by the likes of Mark Rothko, Pablo Picasso, and Barnett Newman that also needed a new temporary home.

Chez Matisse – Masterpieces from the Centre Pompidou, comprises some 80 works, including La Blouse roumaine, which is hardly ever allowed off the Pompidou premises. The collection follows Matisse as he experimented with colour and shapes, culminating in his work at the Chapelle du Rosaire in Vence. From October 3. Website

Catch a De Kooning
The Rijksmuseum blockbuster this autumn is a retrospective of Dutch abstract expressionist painter Willem de Kooning (1904-1997) which puts his drawings centre stage. De Kooning left his native Rotterdam at age 24 and entered the United States as a stowaway. Willem de Kooning at work shows over 120 drawings, and some of his sculptures and paintings, mapping out De Kooning’s journey from house painter to important innovator of modern art. From October 6. Website

Get a taste of Japan in The Hague
The Japanese Garden at the Clingendael Estate in The Hague, which opens for a few weeks every year, is more popular than ever. Make sure you get your ticket for a slot to see its autumnal splendour. From October 10. Website

Cock a snoot at speculators
Plus ça change…Cherry Town is a jolly musical romp about housing shortage, corruption and the healing power of love, based on the operetta by Russian composer Dmitri Shostakovich written in 1959. Performed by the Dutch National Opera and supported by the Netherlands Philharmonic, the comical shenanigans of speculators and indignant tenants are a treat for young (from 10) and old. Sung in English. October 8-20. Website

Remember Marisol
The Boijmans van Beuningen museum in Rotterdam has dusted off the largely forgotten work of Marisol (1930-2016), a Venezuelan artist whose playful wooden sculptures about serious subjects, such as women’s rights and the environment, became popular in the 1960s. The museum organised her first solo show and The Car became one of its most celebrated exhibits. From October 9. Website

Say hello to Whistler’s mum
Van Gogh liked and wrote about many of his contemporaries, including James Whistler, which spurred the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam to organise the major retrospective Whistler, Dandy and Disruptor. The dandy bit refers to his dashing looks while his l’art pour l’art attitude upset the critics of the time.

His most famous painting Arrangement in Gray and Black, No. 1, better known, to his annoyance, as Whistler’s Mother, moved Van Gogh, who said it reminded him of his own mother. From October 16. Website

..and see his take on Amsterdam
At the same time as the main exhibition in Amsterdam, the Mesdag Collection in The Hague presents Whistler. Loving the Netherlands. The painter visited the Netherlands 10 times, resulting in etchings and atmospheric watercolours.

With dandyish good taste, he chastised his Dutch fellow artists: “You Dutch painters don’t know what you’re missing by neglecting your beautiful city of Amsterdam, which I find more beautiful than Venice.”  From October 16. Website

Explore some great design ideas
Dutch Design Week is ‘returning to RAW or Rebel Authentic Worth, unpolished and real”, so prepare to get basic. The Sausage Stool (Wuerstelhocker), a sausage-shaped perch on which to enjoy a wuerstel (and future sausage stool), is a case in point.

Eindhoven becomes the focal point of international creative ideas on serious subjects such as sustainability, new materials, technology,  education, play and much, much more. October 17-25. Website

Get to know Eve at the Vrijthof
The Fotomuseum aan het Vrijthof in Maastricht presents All About Eve, a retrospective of celebrated Magnum photographer Eve Arnold. The selection of 150 photographs focuses on her work from the 50s, 60s and 70s and includes images of famous filmstars and several series, including Malcolm X and Fashion Shows in Harlem. From October 19. Website

Get a buzz at the ADE
The 30th edition of the electronic music festival Amsterdam Dance Event is about to be unleashed on the capital, featuring, among many others, the Concertgebouw Orchestra playing Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony against the background of Einder, an artificial and ever-changing sky of floaty fabric covering the vast Centrale Markthal.

The ADE is also putting in a special appearance at the Van Gogh Museum (see above) on October 23, when electronic music band Devon Rexi and musician Coby Sey will respond electronically to Whistler’s work Nocturnes. October 21-25. Website

item.title: Young Amsterdammers drink less as ketamine gains ground
item.description:
Young Amsterdammers drink less as ketamine gains ground

October 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Young people in Amsterdam are drinking less alcohol, but drugs like ketamine have become far more popular at the same time, according to an annual monitor of drug and alcohol use commissioned by addiction care organisation Jellinek.

The researchers say Gen Z drinks less often and more consciously, partly because of rising prices.

The Antenne Amsterdam 2025 report was published on Wednesday by the Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences (HvA). It draws on a survey of 1,183 vocational college (mbo) students, interviews with 22 nightlife insiders and five youth workers, and close to 5,000 drug samples handed in to testing services.

Of the students surveyed, 59% had drunk alcohol in the past year and 46% in the past four weeks. Both figures are lower than among their peers at hbo colleges and universities.

Ketamine on the rise
Ketamine use is widespread in Amsterdam’s nightlife and has risen sharply again since 2024, the report says. Ketamine, MDMA and other powder drugs are relatively cheap, going for €25-30 per gram, and are easily obtained via home delivery services.

Demand for 3-MMC, a synthetic stimulant, appears barely affected by a ban on several groups of related substances that took effect on July 1 last year. Drugs sold as 3-MMC often turn out to contain other substances, such as 2-MMC.

Among vocational students, however, 3-MMC is relatively rare: 7% have ever tried it and 5% used it in the past year. Laughing gas has almost disappeared since the sales ban. Just 9% of students said they had ever used it, down from 24% in 2021.

Vaping and gambling
Fewer students smoke than in previous years, but nicotine products remain popular. Some 24% smoke, 18% vaped in the past four weeks, and 7% used nicotine pouches, known as snus.

The share of students who gambled online in the past year has tripled, from 6% in 2021 to 18%. The researchers caution that the question was worded differently in 2025.

Less drinking is a positive development but it brings new concerns, Jellinek prevention specialist Raoul Koning said in a statement. He named vaping, snus, 3-MMC, ketamine, and gambling as particular problems.

If you are concerned about your own or someone else’s use of alcohol, drugs, or gambling, the Jellinek addiction helpline can be reached on 088 505 1220 or at jellinek.nl. The line is staffed in Dutch and English on weekdays, 1pm to 5pm.

item.title: EU halts aid funds to Sierra Leone over Bolle Jos extradition
item.description:
EU halts aid funds to Sierra Leone over Bolle Jos extradition

October 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The European Commission has stopped payments to Sierra Leone with immediate effect because the country will not extradite fugitive drugs baron Jos Leijdekkers, known as Bolle Jos, justice minister David van Weel has confirmed.

Van Weel told De Telegraaf: “I am very happy with this step. It is galling that EU money goes to a country that does not want to cooperate with the extradition of someone like Bolle Jos.”

Jos reportedly has a child with the daughter of Sierra Leone’s president, Julius Maada Bio, and maintains close ties with the government there. Drugs shipments passing through the West African coast are an increasing concern, for which Van Weel wants to establish a permanent secretariat.

Sierra Leone was expected to receive €18 million euros in budget support from Europe this year, most of it intended to bolster education, food programs and infrastructure projects. The Netherlands is also hoping to stop a planned payment of €22.5 million to the country next year.

Van Weel travelled to West Africa recently to garner support from surrounding nations like Ghana and Liberia.

Van Weel is in Luxembourg on Thursday for a meeting with EU justice ministers, where tougher sanctions on criminals hiding outside Europe, such as entry bans and asset freezes, will be discussed.

Pressure to tackle the cocaine trade has grown since an armed attack on a farm in Overasselt, Gelderland, last month, in which a security guard was killed. The attack is thought to be linked to the drugs trade.

item.title: Clitoris reconstruction surgery successful at Radboudumc
item.description:
Clitoris reconstruction surgery successful at Radboudumc

October 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Doctors at Radboudumc have successfully completed clitoral reconstruction surgeries in women who lost part of the sex organ to vulvar cancer, including restoring their ability to orgasm.

In a statement, the hospital in Nijmegen said that of 23 women who underwent the procedure, 90% were able to experience a clitoral orgasm again.

In the Netherlands, approximately 450 women are diagnosed with vulvar cancer every year. In around 25% of those cases, the clitoris or the surrounding area is affected.

In patients whose tumour is located on or near the clitoris, part of the organ may need to be removed.

“Until now, the wound was closed afterwards and the clitoris disappeared under a layer of skin, without regard for quality of life or the question of whether an orgasm is still possible,” gynecological oncologist Mieke ten Eikelder said.

This advancement has happened almost 40 years after similar surgery for the penis. The first reconstructive surgery for the penis after cancer dates back to 1987.

Clitoral reconstruction is now being rolled out nationwide as part of scientific research.

item.title: Curaçao refused Machado flight after request “from higher up”
item.description:
Curaçao refused Machado flight after request “from higher up”

October 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Curaçao’s aviation authority refused landing permission for a plane carrying Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado on her way back to Venezuela last week after a “request from higher up”, the authority’s director told broadcaster NOS.

Peter Steinmetz, head of the Curaçao Civil Aviation Authority (CCAA), did not say who made the request. Ministers in Willemstad and The Hague have also not commented on who made it.

The private plane was due to fly from Panama, where Machado is living, to Curaçao on September 22. An attempt to fly her to Aruba the same day also fell through. Journalists travelling with Machado said at the time that the flights had been cancelled because of problems with paperwork.

Machado won the Nobel peace prize last year for her efforts in opposing Venezuela’s former president Nicolás Maduro, who was captured by US forces in January. US policy is officially neutral on whether she should return, Axios reported in July, adding that her repeated attempts had angered senior officials in the Trump administration.

Who made the request?
The island’s prime minister Gilmar Pisas declined to comment, and the national transport minister Charles Cooper said the request did not come from him.

Curaçao controls its own civil aviation, but foreign policy is a joint matter for the whole Kingdom of the Netherlands.

Eric van der Burg, the Dutch junior minister for kingdom relations, told Caribbean media that foreign minister Tom Berendsen would speak on the issue, calling it “a very delicate situation.”

According to NOS, the decision was taken by the kingdom council of ministers, which brings together the Dutch cabinet and ministers from Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten.

Berendsen attended a meeting of the council on September 25, three days after the flights were refused. Prime minister Rob Jetten declined to rule out Dutch involvement at his weekly press conference last week.

Unanswered questions
It remains unclear whether the request came from Curaçao, the Netherlands or another government.

Earlier this week, Leiden university professor Wouter Veenendaal, who specialises in relations between the nations in the Kingdom of the Netherlands, told Dutch News: “I can’t prove it, but it sounds to me like The Hague has been put under pressure by the Americans.”

“Although the Americans formally take a positive view of Machado, her arrival is seen as potentially threatening the relative stability that they’ve been able to create with the interim president.”

Machado’s team says she has made at least seven attempts to return to Venezuela.

Dutch News has asked the foreign affairs ministry who made the request and whether the Netherlands was involved. The ministry had not responded at the time of publication.

item.title: Writer and cabaret performer Paulien Cornelisse dies at age 50
item.description:
Writer and cabaret performer Paulien Cornelisse dies at age 50

October 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Celebrated writer and cabaret performer Paulien Cornelisse, known for her popular books about the Dutch language, died on Wednesday of cancer.

The 50-year-old was a jury chair on the popular TV quiz show De Slimste Mens as well as authoring a number of books, including Taal is zeg maar echt mijn ding or Language is really my thing.

She announced in 2024 that she had been diagnosed with cancer. During an appearance on De Slimste Mens last month she wore a blue beanie to cover her head after losing her hair to chemotherapy.

Broadcaster KRO-NCRV announced on Wednesday that the evening’s episode of De Slimste Mens would be cancelled.

“I am incredibly sad. Paulien was sweet, funny, and also – between treatments – greatly energetic,” her co-host Herman van der Zandt said in a statement.

Cornelisse began her career as a cabaret performer. In 2008, Taal is zeg maar echt mijn ding was published and became a bestseller, with over 700,000 copies sold.

She later wrote absurdist novels about a guinea pig working in an office, starting with De verwarde cavia (The Confused Guinea Pig), which was also a bestseller. The follow-up, De verwarde cavia – Terug op kantoor (The Confused Guinea Pig – Back at the Office), won the NS Public Prize last year.

She wrote a weekly column about language for the NRC for 10 years, and had been a front-page columnist for the Volkskrant since 2018.

Volkskrant editor-in-chief Pieter Klok said her death was “a loss for the whole of the Netherlands.”

Cornelisse was born and raised in Amsterdam. The city’s mayor Femke Halsema wrote in a post on social media that she was someone “who loved the small, the everyday, the absurd, and the theatre.”

“Sadly, that stage was no longer granted to her,” Halsema said.

item.title: Fines for “advertising” slimming drugs triggered by competitor
item.description:
Fines for “advertising” slimming drugs triggered by competitor

September 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

An investigation into Dutch media coverage of weight loss drugs that led to several outlets being fined for breaching advertising laws was prompted by a complaint from a rival manufacturer, NRC reports.

Newspapers including NRC, the Telegraaf, the Volkskrant and AD were sanctioned by the health inspectorate IGJ in August, when it ruled that articles about medicines such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro were too positive.

NRC said its lawyers had discovered that the IGJ acted after being asked to enforce the Medicines Act, which bans advertising of prescription drugs, by Goodlife, which manufacturers the slimming drug Mysimba.

One of Goodlife’s objections was that the artlcles in NRC and the Volkskrant were unbalanced because of the “complete absence of references to Mysimba in the majority of media reports”.

The Dutch Medicines Act was passed in 1992 to protect public health by banning commercial companies from advertising drugs that are only available on prescription. In many countries drugs such as Ozempic are used for weight loss, but doctors in the Netherlands are only allowed to prescribe them for diabetes.

Commercial battle

Lucas Brouwers, deputy editor of NRC, said: “Apparently the IGJ did not chance upon the articles in NRC itself, but was pointed towards them by a company that sells a rival slimming medicine.

“We are very concerned that the media are being dragged into a commercial battle through the inspectorate.”

Volkskrant editor Pieter Klok said if the fines were upheld, it would make it almost imposslble for health reporters to write about developments in medical treatment.

“This makes it even worse,” he said. “I already had major objections on principle, but now it is becoming very arbitrary. The IGJ must not allow itself to be used by competing parties.”

Maartenm Kok, medical director of Goodlife, told NRC that reporting on obesity treatments in the Dutch media “gave a one-sided and incomplete picture in which only a limited number of medicines were repeatedly and overwhelmingly positively highlighted.“

Nieuwsuur threatened

DPG Media and Mediahuis, the owners of the newspaper titles, are appealing against the fines.

Goodlife also asked the IGJ to investigate TV current affairs show Nieuwsuur after it broadcast a four-part series into the effects of medicines such as Ozempic that work by simulating the effect of the natural hormone GLP-1, which tells the brain the stomach is full.

The company threatened to seek an injunction against the programme after reporter Lune van der Meulen rejected its demand to include Mysimba in the series, but dropped the action after she said on air she had been contacted by a distributor.

item.title: Unconditional jail demanded for attacks on emergency workers
item.description:
Unconditional jail demanded for attacks on emergency workers

September 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

People who attack emergency workers, including police officers, paramedics and train staff, will face an unconditional prison sentence from Thursday, under new rules from the public prosecution service (OM).

Prosecutors will no longer settle such cases with a fine or community service, and every suspect will have to appear in court, the OM said on Wednesday. The rules will apply to offences committed from October 1.

It sets fixed sentencing guidelines for three offences: public violence, assault, and attempted serious assault. An attempt to seriously assault an emergency worker without a weapon and without causing injury, for example, will carry a demand of 3 months in prison.

Justice minister David van Weel told MPs that a similar attack on a member of the public would usually lead to a demand for 80 hours community service, broadcaster NOS reported.

Besides emergency workers, the rules cover security staff, sports referees, public transport workers, teachers, judges, lawyers, politicians and council staff. They also apply to attacks on journalists.

“The impact of this violence on society is huge, but unfortunately we are not seeing it decline,” Lisan Wösten, the OM’s national lead on the issue, said in a statement.

Pressure from MPs
MPs called for tougher sentences early this year after police and firefighters were attacked at New Year, with officers in some places lured into ambushes. “I fully support that approach,” Van Weel wrote in his letter to parliament, according to NOS.

Police officers faced almost 13,000 violent incidents in 2025, and the force’s national lead on the issue, Corry van Breda, has called for heavier sentences.

Since 2006, prosecutors have been able to seek sentences 200% higher for attacks on people in public roles. However, research by the justice ministry’s research centre WODC found this was rarely applied in practice.

The new rules remain a starting point from which prosecutors and judges can still exercise discretion according to the circumstances of a case.

A separate proposal to ban community service for these attacks altogether was criticised last year by the Council of State and judges, who said it would limit their room to weigh individual circumstances.
